Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Assessment: Female, 45 years old, with painful, cracked, itchy palms with occasional bleeding (when scratched), gradually worsening over 3–4 months since starting a new housekeeping job where she routinely handles cleaning products without gloves. Mild dryness also noted on legs. No significant past dermatologic history. Medical history includes type 2 diabetes (controlled on metformin).
- The presentation, with a clear occupational temporal relationship and failure to improve with over-the-counter emollients and antihistamines, is consistent with irritant contact dermatitis.
- Allergic contact dermatitis is considered but less likely based on history (no prior atopy; classic irritant pattern). 
- No systemic features or suspicion for infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease.
- No evidence to suggest diabetic skin infection, atopic eczema, or fungal infection.
- No examination or laboratory findings recorded.
- Plan (per transcript): Advise strict avoidance of triggers (consistent glove use at work). Prescribe topical steroid cream and stronger emollients (to be applied 3–4 times daily for 10–14 days). Review in 1–2 weeks if not improved or sooner if symptoms worsen or spread.

Management Plan
- Advise wearing protective gloves at all times during cleaning activities.
- Prescribe topical steroid cream (dose/route/frequency not documented) and stronger emollients (to be used as described above).
- Arrange prescription with pharmacy.
- Advise follow-up in 1–2 weeks if no improvement, or sooner if symptoms worsen.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Irritant contact dermatitis – High likelihood. Justified by strong occupational exposure (cleaning chemicals, inconsistent glove use), anatomical location (palms), and time course following job change; symptoms fit classic irritant pattern; not responsive to emollients/antihistamines.
- Allergic contact dermatitis – Moderate likelihood. Occupational exposure and pruritus could suggest allergy, but history and distribution are more consistent with irritant dermatitis.
- Atopic eczema – Low likelihood. Some generalized dryness and pruritus, but lacks atopic history, onset is related to occupation/job change.
